Homework 02

Question 1: Training and test error under a fixed design

Consider a linear regression problem with n=100n=100 observations and p=20p=20 available covariates. Generate one matrix 𝑿all∈ℝn×p\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\in\mathbb R^{n\times p} whose entries are independent 𝒩(0,1)\mathcal N(0,1) random variables, and then keep this realized matrix fixed. Let

βj=0.4j,j=1,…,p, \beta_j=0.4^{\sqrt{j}}, \qquad j=1,\ldots,p,

and define

𝝁=𝑿all𝜷. \boldsymbol\mu=\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\boldsymbol\beta.

Generate one training response and one independent test response from

𝒚=𝝁+𝝐,𝒚*=𝝁+𝝐*, \begin{aligned} \mathbf y &=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\epsilon,\\ \mathbf y^* &=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\epsilon^*, \end{aligned}

where

𝝐,𝝐*∼ind𝒩n(𝟎,𝑰n). \boldsymbol\epsilon,\boldsymbol\epsilon^* \overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim} \mathcal N_n(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I_n).

Here 𝑰n\mathbf I_n is the n×nn\times n identity matrix.

For m=0,1,…,pm=0,1,\ldots,p, fit a linear model with an intercept and the first mm columns of 𝑿all\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}} using 𝒚\mathbf y. If 𝒚̂m\widehat{\mathbf y}_m is its fitted mean vector, define

MSE⁡train,m=1n∥𝒚−𝒚̂m∥22, \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train},m} =\frac{1}{n} \left\lVert \mathbf y-\widehat{\mathbf y}_m \right\rVert_2^2,

and

MSE⁡test,m=1n∥𝒚*−𝒚̂m∥22. \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test},m} =\frac{1}{n} \left\lVert \mathbf y^*-\widehat{\mathbf y}_m \right\rVert_2^2.

Repeat this process independently 200 times, keeping 𝑿all\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}} fixed.

Use seed 43202 before generating 𝑿all\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}} and the response errors. R and Python use different random-number generators, so their exact numerical values need not agree.

  1. For each mm, calculate the average training and test MSE over the 200 simulation runs. Plot both curves against mm. Verify numerically that training MSE does not increase as predictors are added in each simulation run.

  2. For the model containing the first mm predictors, write

𝑿m=[𝟏,𝒙1,…,𝒙m],𝑯m=𝑿m(𝑿m𝖳𝑿m)−1𝑿m𝖳. \mathbf X_m = [\mathbf 1,\mathbf x_1,\ldots,\mathbf x_m], \qquad \mathbf H_m = \mathbf X_m (\mathbf X_m^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X_m)^{-1} \mathbf X_m^{\mathsf T}.

Here 𝑿m∈ℝn×(m+1)\mathbf X_m\in\mathbb R^{n\times(m+1)} and 𝑯m∈ℝn×n\mathbf H_m\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}. The model has m+1m+1 fitted coefficients, including the intercept. Define its total squared approximation bias as

Bm2=∥(𝑰n−𝑯m)𝝁∥22. B_m^2 =\left\lVert (\mathbf I_n-\mathbf H_m)\boldsymbol\mu \right\rVert_2^2.

Thus, Bm2/nB_m^2/n is the mean squared approximation bias.

Calculate the two theoretical expectations

E(MSE⁡train,m∣𝑿all)=Bm2n+1−m+1n, E\!\left( \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train},m} \mid \mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}} \right) =\frac{B_m^2}{n}+1-\frac{m+1}{n},

and

E(MSE⁡test,m∣𝑿all)=Bm2n+1+m+1n. E\!\left( \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test},m} \mid \mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}} \right) =\frac{B_m^2}{n}+1+\frac{m+1}{n}.

Add these expectations to your plot and compare them with the simulation averages.

  1. Add the test MSE curve from one simulation run to the plot. Explain why this single curve is less smooth than the average test MSE. Use the approximation-bias and estimation-variance terms in the expected test MSE to explain why training MSE cannot be used by itself to select the predictor count.

Show the starter code 
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(43202)
n = 100
p = 20
repetitions = 200
 
# Generate one covariate matrix, then keep it fixed.
X_all = rng.normal(size=(n, p))
beta = 0.4 ** np.sqrt(np.arange(1, p + 1))
mu = X_all @ beta
 
# Rows are repetitions; columns are predictor counts 0 through p.
train_mse = np.empty((repetitions, p + 1))
test_mse = np.empty((repetitions, p + 1))
 
# Each run observes a fresh training and test response.
for k in range(repetitions):
    y_train = mu + rng.normal(size=n)
    y_test = mu + rng.normal(size=n)
 
    # Compare every candidate model on this same response pair.
    for m in range(p + 1):
        X_m = np.column_stack((np.ones(n), X_all[:, :m]))
        Q = np.linalg.qr(X_m, mode="reduced")[0]
        y_hat = Q @ (Q.T @ y_train)
 
        train_mse[k, m] = np.mean((y_train - y_hat) ** 2)
        test_mse[k, m] = np.mean((y_test - y_hat) ** 2)
 
average_train = train_mse.mean(axis=0)
average_test = test_mse.mean(axis=0)
 
training_is_monotone = np.all(np.diff(train_mse, axis=1) <= 1e-10)
 
print("=== Part (a) ===")
for m in [0, 5, 10, 15, 20]:
    print(f"m={m:2d}, average train={average_train[m]:.4f}, average test={average_test[m]:.4f}")
print("Training MSE is monotone across all 200 runs:", training_is_monotone)
=== Part (a) ===
m= 0, average train=1.3220, average test=1.3416
m= 5, average train=0.9976, average test=1.1107
m=10, average train=0.8960, average test=1.1218
m=15, average train=0.8446, average test=1.1605
m=20, average train=0.7889, average test=1.2119
Training MSE is monotone across all 200 runs: True

Training MSE decreases monotonically across all 200 runs (training_is_monotone = True) — adding a predictor can only shrink the residual sum of squares of a least-squares fit, since the larger model space always contains the smaller one as a special case. Average test MSE, by contrast, decreases at first (more predictors reduce bias) then rises again once added variance from estimating extra coefficients outweighs the bias reduction.

Show the starter code 
theory_train = np.empty(p + 1)
theory_test = np.empty(p + 1)
 
for m in range(p + 1):
    X_m = np.column_stack((np.ones(n), X_all[:, :m]))
    Q = np.linalg.qr(X_m, mode="reduced")[0]
    y_hat = Q @ (Q.T @ mu)
    bias_mse = np.mean((mu - y_hat) ** 2)
    theory_train[m] = bias_mse + 1 - (m + 1) / n
    theory_test[m] = bias_mse + 1 + (m + 1) / n
 
print("\n=== Part (b) ===")
for m in [0, 5, 10, 15, 20]:
    print(
        f"m={m:2d}, "
        f"train={average_train[m]:.4f} vs E(train)={theory_train[m]:.4f}, "
        f"test={average_test[m]:.4f} vs E(test)={theory_test[m]:.4f}"
    )
print("Minimum average test MSE at m =", int(np.argmin(average_test)))
print("Minimum expected test MSE at m =", int(np.argmin(theory_test)))

=== Part (b) ===
m= 0, train=1.3220 vs E(train)=1.3078, test=1.3416 vs E(test)=1.3278
m= 5, train=0.9976 vs E(train)=0.9894, test=1.1107 vs E(test)=1.1094
m=10, train=0.8960 vs E(train)=0.8980, test=1.1218 vs E(test)=1.1180
m=15, train=0.8446 vs E(train)=0.8419, test=1.1605 vs E(test)=1.1619
m=20, train=0.7889 vs E(train)=0.7900, test=1.2119 vs E(test)=1.2100
Minimum average test MSE at m = 7
Minimum expected test MSE at m = 7

The simulation averages track the theoretical curves closely at every m shown (e.g., at m=10: 0.896 vs 0.898 train, 1.122 vs 1.118 test). Both the simulated and theoretical test MSE are minimized at m = 7, confirming the bias–variance tradeoff formula E(MSE_test) = B²_m/n + 1 + (m+1)/n correctly predicts where the interior minimum occurs.

Show the starter code 
first_run_test = test_mse[0]

print("\n=== Part (c) ===")
print("Single-run (repetition 1) test MSE at m=0,5,10,15,20:",
      [round(first_run_test[m], 4) for m in [0, 5, 10, 15, 20]])
 
# Final plot combining all three parts
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.2))
m_values = np.arange(p + 1)
ax.plot(m_values, average_train, color="#2F6FB3", lw=2.3, label="Average training")
ax.plot(m_values, theory_train, "--", color="#2F6FB3", lw=2, label="Expected training")
ax.plot(m_values, average_test, color="#C84A16", lw=2.3, label="Average test")
ax.plot(m_values, theory_test, "--", color="#C84A16", lw=2, label="Expected test")
ax.plot(m_values, first_run_test, ":", color="0.45", lw=1.4, label="Test, repetition 1")
ax.set(xlabel="Number of predictors", ylabel="Mean squared error")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

=== Part (c) ===
Single-run (repetition 1) test MSE at m=0,5,10,15,20: [np.float64(1.1288), np.float64(0.7858), np.float64(0.8244), np.float64(0.77), np.float64(0.7858)]

The single-run test curve is jagged because it reflects one realized noise vector ε*, which doesn’t shrink or grow systematically with m — it just adds random wiggle on top of the true trend. Averaging over 200 runs cancels that noise, leaving the smooth expected curve. This also shows why training MSE alone can’t be used to choose m: it’s monotonically decreasing by construction and has no way to “see” the (m+1)/n variance penalty that eventually makes larger models generalize worse — only test MSE (or its theoretical decomposition) captures that tradeoff.

Question 2: Prediction error at one target point

Let n=100n=100, p=6p=6, and σ2=1\sigma^2=1. Construct the fixed covariate matrix 𝑿all∈ℝn×p\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\in\mathbb R^{n\times p} with entries

(𝑿all)ij=2cos⁡{πj(i−12)n},i=1,…,n,j=1,…,p. (\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}})_{ij} =\sqrt{2}\cos\left\{ \frac{\pi j(i-\tfrac12)}{n} \right\}, \qquad i=1,\ldots,n, \quad j=1,\ldots,p.

Its columns satisfy

𝟏𝖳𝑿all=𝟎𝖳,1n𝑿all𝖳𝑿all=𝑰p. \mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}=\mathbf 0^{\mathsf T}, \qquad \frac{1}{n}\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}=\mathbf I_p.

Here 𝑰p\mathbf I_p is the p×pp\times p identity matrix.

The following code shows a direct construction of 𝑿all\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}.

  • R
  • Python
#| eval: false
n <- 100
p <- 6
X_all <- outer(
  1:n, 1:p,
  function(i, j) sqrt(2) * cos(pi * j * (i - 0.5) / n)
)
Show the starter code 
import numpy as np

n, p = 100, 6
i = np.arange(1, n + 1)[:, None]
j = np.arange(1, p + 1)[None, :]
X_all = np.sqrt(2) * np.cos(np.pi * j * (i - 0.5) / n)

Keep 𝑿all\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}} fixed and generate one training response from

𝒚=𝑿all𝜷+𝝐,𝜷=(0.5,0.5,0.5,0.5,0.5,0.5)𝖳, \mathbf y =\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon, \qquad \boldsymbol\beta =(0.5,0.5,0.5,0.5,0.5,0.5)^{\mathsf T},

where

𝝐∼𝒩n(𝟎,𝑰n). \boldsymbol\epsilon \sim \mathcal N_n(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I_n).

Here 𝑰n\mathbf I_n is the n×nn\times n identity matrix.

For m=0,…,pm=0,\ldots,p, fit a linear model with an intercept and the first mm predictors. Consider prediction of the mean response at

𝒙0=(0,1,0,0,1,0)𝖳. \mathbf x_0=(0,1,0,0,1,0)^{\mathsf T}.

Write

μ0=𝒙0𝖳𝜷, \mu_0=\mathbf x_0^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta,

and let μ̂0,m\widehat\mu_{0,m} be the prediction from the model containing the first mm predictors. Here x0jx_{0j} denotes the jjth coordinate of 𝒙0\mathbf x_0. For this design,

E[(μ̂0,m−μ0)2∣𝑿all]=(∑j=m+1px0jβj)2+σ2n(1+∑j=1mx0j2). E\!\left[ \left(\widehat\mu_{0,m}-\mu_0\right)^2 \mid \mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}} \right] = \left( \sum_{j=m+1}^{p}x_{0j}\beta_j \right)^2 +\frac{\sigma^2}{n} \left( 1+\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_{0j}^2 \right).

  1. Calculate μ0\mu_0, the theoretical squared bias, and the expected squared error for m=0,…,pm=0,\ldots,p using the formula above. You do not need to derive the formula. Briefly explain in words why it consists of a squared bias term from omitted predictors and a variance term from estimating coefficients; no proof is required. Identify the values of mm where the expected squared error changes and where it remains unchanged.

  2. Use seed 43203. Generate the response, fit the models, and calculate

(μ̂0,m−μ0)2. \left(\widehat\mu_{0,m}-\mu_0\right)^2.

Repeat this independently 200 times. Plot the simulation averages and theoretical expectations together. Report the smallest mm that minimizes the theoretical error.

  1. All six regression coefficients are nonzero. Explain why only predictors 2 and 5 contribute directly to the mean response at 𝒙0\mathbf x_0. Contrast this target-specific error with the test MSE averaged over all rows of 𝑿all\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}} in Question 1.

Show the starter code 
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

n = 100
p = 6
sigma2 = 1.0
repetitions = 200
 
i = np.arange(1, n + 1)[:, None]
j = np.arange(1, p + 1)[None, :]
X_all = np.sqrt(2) * np.cos(np.pi * j * (i - 0.5) / n)
 
beta = np.repeat(0.5, p)
x0 = np.array([0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0], dtype=float)
mu = X_all @ beta
mu0 = x0 @ beta

assert np.allclose(X_all.sum(axis=0), 0, atol=1e-10)
assert np.allclose(X_all.T @ X_all / n, np.eye(p), atol=1e-10)
 
theoretical = np.empty(p + 1)
squared_bias = np.empty(p + 1)
variance_term = np.empty(p + 1)
 
for m in range(p + 1):
    omitted_signal = x0[m:] @ beta[m:]          # bias contribution: coefficients not yet in the model
    estimation_variance = sigma2 * (1 + x0[:m] @ x0[:m]) / n  # variance from estimating m coefficients + intercept
    squared_bias[m] = omitted_signal**2
    variance_term[m] = estimation_variance
    theoretical[m] = squared_bias[m] + variance_term[m]
 
print("=== Part (a) ===")
print(f"mu_0 = {mu0:.4f}")
for m in range(p + 1):
    print(
        f"m={m}, squared bias={squared_bias[m]:.4f}, "
        f"variance term={variance_term[m]:.4f}, "
        f"E[(mu0_hat - mu0)^2]={theoretical[m]:.4f}"
    )
=== Part (a) ===
mu_0 = 1.0000
m=0, squared bias=1.0000, variance term=0.0100, E[(mu0_hat - mu0)^2]=1.0100
m=1, squared bias=1.0000, variance term=0.0100, E[(mu0_hat - mu0)^2]=1.0100
m=2, squared bias=0.2500, variance term=0.0200, E[(mu0_hat - mu0)^2]=0.2700
m=3, squared bias=0.2500, variance term=0.0200, E[(mu0_hat - mu0)^2]=0.2700
m=4, squared bias=0.2500, variance term=0.0200, E[(mu0_hat - mu0)^2]=0.2700
m=5, squared bias=0.0000, variance term=0.0300, E[(mu0_hat - mu0)^2]=0.0300
m=6, squared bias=0.0000, variance term=0.0300, E[(mu0_hat - mu0)^2]=0.0300

μ₀ = x₀ᵀβ = 1(0.5) + 1(0.5) = 1.0000 (only positions 2 and 5 of x₀ are nonzero, each contributing 0.5). The error decomposes into a squared bias term — the squared sum of coefficients for predictors not yet in the model (since a left-out true signal biases the prediction) — plus a variance term that grows with m because each additional coefficient estimated from noisy data adds estimation variance, scaled by (1+∑x₀ⱼ²)/n. The expected squared error only changes at m=2 and m=5 — the two points where a nonzero-β predictor (2 or 5) enters the model and knocks out part of the bias. At m=0→1, m=2→3→4, and m=5→6, the error is flat, because predictors 1, 3, 4, and 6 have x₀ⱼ=0, so including them adds variance without reducing bias at all — pure waste for this specific target.

Show the starter code 
rng_q2 = np.random.default_rng(43203)
 
# Rows are repetitions; columns are predictor counts 0 through p.
simulation_error = np.empty((repetitions, p + 1))
 
# Each run observes a fresh response.
for k in range(repetitions):
    y_train = mu + rng_q2.normal(size=n)
 
    # Compare every candidate model on this same response.
    for m in range(p + 1):
        X_m = np.column_stack((np.ones(n), X_all[:, :m]))
        beta_hat = np.linalg.solve(X_m.T @ X_m, X_m.T @ y_train)
        target_row = np.r_[1, x0[:m]]
        mu0_hat = target_row @ beta_hat
        simulation_error[k, m] = (mu0_hat - mu0) ** 2
 
simulated = simulation_error.mean(axis=0)
 
print("\n=== Part (b) ===")
for m in range(p + 1):
    print(f"m={m}, simulated={simulated[m]:.4f}, theoretical={theoretical[m]:.4f}")
print("Smallest m minimizing theoretical error:", int(np.argmin(theoretical)))
 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
m_values = np.arange(p + 1)
ax.plot(m_values, simulated, "o-", color="#2F6FB3", lw=2.3, label="Simulation average")
ax.plot(m_values, theoretical, "--", color="#C84A16", lw=2, label="Theoretical expectation")
ax.axvline(2, color="0.6", linestyle=":")
ax.axvline(5, color="0.6", linestyle=":")
ax.set(xlabel="Number of predictors", ylabel="Mean squared error at the target", xticks=m_values)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False)

Show the starter code 
print("\n=== Part (c) ===")
print("x0 =", x0)
print("Nonzero entries of x0 at positions (1-indexed):",
      [idx + 1 for idx, val in enumerate(x0) if val != 0])

=== Part (c) ===
x0 = [0. 1. 0. 0. 1. 0.]
Nonzero entries of x0 at positions (1-indexed): [2, 5]

All six β’s are nonzero, but only predictors 2 and 5 have nonzero coordinates in x₀ = (0,1,0,0,1,0)ᵀ — since prediction at this specific point is x₀ᵀβ̂, any coefficient multiplied by a zero coordinate simply doesn’t affect the predicted value, regardless of how well or poorly it’s estimated. This is fundamentally different from Question 1’s test MSE, which averages error over every row of X_all — there, all 20 predictors eventually matter because different test observations have nonzero values in different coordinates. Here we’re asking about one fixed point, so only the coordinates that are actually nonzero at that point can influence bias; everything else is only ever a variance cost.

Question 3: The optimism correction

Choose one candidate model before observing the response. Let pp be its number of predictors and let 𝑿∈ℝn×(p+1)\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times(p+1)} be its full-rank design matrix, including the intercept. The model has p+1p+1 fitted coefficients. Let

𝑯=𝑿(𝑿𝖳𝑿)−1𝑿𝖳 \mathbf H =\mathbf X (\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1} \mathbf X^{\mathsf T}

be its hat matrix. Suppose

𝒚=𝝁+𝝐,𝒚*=𝝁+𝝐*, \mathbf y=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\epsilon, \qquad \mathbf y^*=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\epsilon^*,

Conditional on the fixed design 𝑿\mathbf X, the two error vectors are independent, have mean zero, and have covariance matrix σ2𝑰n\sigma^2\mathbf I_n. Define

MSE⁡train=1n∥𝒚−𝑯𝒚∥22,MSE⁡test=1n∥𝒚*−𝑯𝒚∥22. \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train}} = \frac{1}{n} \left\lVert \mathbf y-\mathbf H\mathbf y \right\rVert_2^2, \qquad \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}} = \frac{1}{n} \left\lVert \mathbf y^*-\mathbf H\mathbf y \right\rVert_2^2.

The conditional bias vector of the fitted mean is

E(𝑯𝒚∣𝑿)−𝝁=−(𝑰n−𝑯)𝝁. E(\mathbf H\mathbf y\mid\mathbf X)-\boldsymbol\mu = -(\mathbf I_n-\mathbf H)\boldsymbol\mu.

Let B2B^2 denote the total squared approximation bias:

B2=∥(𝑰n−𝑯)𝝁∥22. B^2 =\left\lVert (\mathbf I_n-\mathbf H)\boldsymbol\mu \right\rVert_2^2.

Thus, B2/nB^2/n is the mean squared approximation bias.

You may use

𝑯𝖳=𝑯,𝑯2=𝑯,tr⁡(𝑯)=p+1. \mathbf H^{\mathsf T}=\mathbf H, \qquad \mathbf H^2=\mathbf H, \qquad \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf H)=p+1.

For any fixed matrix 𝑨\mathbf A, you may also use

E(𝝐𝖳𝑨𝝐∣𝑿)=σ2tr⁡(𝑨). E\!\left( \boldsymbol\epsilon^{\mathsf T} \mathbf A \boldsymbol\epsilon \mid \mathbf X \right) =\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf A).

  1. Derive

E(MSE⁡train∣𝑿)=B2n+σ2(1−p+1n), E(\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train}}\mid\mathbf X) =\frac{B^2}{n} +\sigma^2\left(1-\frac{p+1}{n}\right),

and

E(MSE⁡test∣𝑿)=B2n+σ2(1+p+1n). E(\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}}\mid\mathbf X) =\frac{B^2}{n} +\sigma^2\left(1+\frac{p+1}{n}\right).

  1. Deduce the expected optimism, defined as E(MSE⁡test−MSE⁡train∣𝑿)E(\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}}-\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train}}\mid\mathbf X). For

n=120,p=4,B2n=0.04,σ2=1, n=120, \qquad p=4, \qquad \frac{B^2}{n}=0.04, \qquad \sigma^2=1,

calculate the expected training MSE, expected test MSE, and their difference. Explain why the ordering need not hold for every realized pair of responses.

  1. Continue with n=120n=120 and p=4p=4. Suppose the candidate model has residual sum of squares RSS⁡=116.4\operatorname{RSS}=116.4, and suppose a common estimate of the error variance is σ̂2=0.96\widehat\sigma^2=0.96.

Calculate

MSÊtest=RSS⁡+2(p+1)σ̂2n, \widehat{\operatorname{MSE}}_{\mathrm{test}} =\frac{ \operatorname{RSS}+2(p+1)\widehat\sigma^2 }{n},

and

Cp=RSSσ̂2−n+2(p+1). C_p =\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{\widehat\sigma^2} -n+2(p+1).

Show how these two quantities are related, and explain why minimizing CpC_p is equivalent to minimizing the corrected test MSE when nn and σ̂2\widehat\sigma^2 are common to all candidate models.

  1. Write y − Hy = (I_n − H)y = (I_n − H)μ + (I_n − H)ε, using y = μ + ε. Since H is symmetric idempotent, so is I_n − H, so (I_n − H)ᵀ(I_n − H) = (I_n − H). Squaring, the cross term with ε vanishes under E(· | X) since E(ε | X) = 0, and the quadratic term becomes E(εᵀ(I_n − H)ε | X) = σ²·tr(I_n − H) = σ²(n − (p + 1)). Combined with ‖(I_n − H)μ‖₂² = B², this gives E(‖y − Hy‖₂² | X) = B² + σ²(n − p − 1), and dividing by n: E(MSE_train | X) = B²/n + σ²(1 − (p+1)/n).

For test error, y* − Hy = (I_n − H)μ + ε* − Hε, where ε* is independent of ε. All cross terms vanish by independence and zero mean, leaving three pieces: ‖(I_n − H)μ‖₂² = B², E(εᵀε | X) = σ²n, and E(εᵀHᵀHε | X) = σ²·tr(H) = σ²(p + 1) (using HᵀH = H). Summing and dividing by n gives E(MSE_test | X) = B²/n + σ²(1 + (p+1)/n).

  1. Subtracting the two results, the B²/n terms cancel, leaving E(MSE_test − MSE_train | X) = 2σ²(p+1)/n — expected optimism depends only on model complexity and noise variance, not bias. Plugging in n = 120, p = 4, B²/n = 0.04, σ² = 1: E(MSE_train | X) = 0.04 + 1·(1 − 5/120) = 0.99833, E(MSE_test | X) = 0.04 + 1·(1 + 5/120) = 1.08167, and optimism = 2(1)(5)/120 = 0.08333 (check: 1.08167 − 0.99833 = 0.08333 ✓).

The ordering only holds in expectation — an average over many hypothetical draws of ε, ε*. For one particular realized sample, MSE_train and MSE_test are random quantities that fluctuate around these means, so a lucky test draw or unlucky training draw can easily flip the inequality for that specific dataset, even though it holds systematically on average across repeated sampling.

  1. Plugging in n = 120, p = 4, RSS = 116.4, σ̂² = 0.96: MSÊ_test = (116.4 + 2(5)(0.96))/120 = 126/120 = 1.05, and C_p = 116.4/0.96 − 120 + 10 = 121.25 − 120 + 10 = 11.25.

To relate them, solve the C_p definition for RSS: RSS = σ̂²(C_p + n − 2(p + 1)), and substitute into MSÊ_test to get MSÊ_test = (σ̂²/n)·C_p + σ̂² (check: (0.96/120)(11.25) + 0.96 = 1.05 ✓). Since n and σ̂² are the same across candidate models, this is a strictly increasing linear function of C_p, which preserves ordering — the model with smallest C_p also has smallest MSÊ_test, so minimizing one is equivalent to minimizing the other.

Question 4: Comparing Mallows’ CpC_p, AIC, and BIC

Use data/diabetes.csv, with y as the response. Use rows 1 through 370 as the training data, and let n=370n=370 denote the training sample size. Do not use rows 371 through 442 in this question. Fit the following ordinary least-squares models, each with an intercept.

Model Predictors pp

Show the starter code 
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
n = 370
train = df.iloc[:n].reset_index(drop=True)
y = train["y"].to_numpy()
 
predictors_A = ["bmi", "bp", "s5", "sex", "s1", "s2", "s4"]
predictors_B = predictors_A + ["s6"]
predictors_full = ["age", "sex", "bmi", "bp", "s1", "s2", "s3", "s4", "s5", "s6"]
 
 
def fit_ols(predictor_names, y):
    """Fit OLS with an intercept; return p (number of predictors) and RSS."""
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y))] + [train[c].to_numpy() for c in predictor_names])
    coef, _, _, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
    resid = y - X @ coef
    rss = float(resid @ resid)
    p = len(predictor_names)
    return p, rss, coef
p_A, rss_A, _ = fit_ols(predictors_A, y)
p_B, rss_B, _ = fit_ols(predictors_B, y)
p_full, rss_full, _ = fit_ols(predictors_full, y)
 
residual_df_full = n - (p_full + 1)
sigma2_hat = rss_full / residual_df_full
 
print("=== Part (a) ===")
print(f"Model A: p={p_A}, RSS={rss_A:.3f}")
print(f"Model B: p={p_B}, RSS={rss_B:.3f}")
print(f"Full   : p={p_full}, RSS={rss_full:.3f}")
print(f"Full model residual df = n - (p+1) = {n} - {p_full + 1} = {residual_df_full}")
print(f"sigma2_hat = RSS_full / residual_df = {sigma2_hat:.6f}")

def criteria(p, rss, n, sigma2_hat):
    cp = rss / sigma2_hat - n + 2 * (p + 1)
    aic_red = n * np.log(rss / n) + 2 * (p + 1)
    bic_red = n * np.log(rss / n) + (p + 1) * np.log(n)
    return cp, aic_red, bic_red
 
cp_A, aic_A, bic_A = criteria(p_A, rss_A, n, sigma2_hat)
cp_B, aic_B, bic_B = criteria(p_B, rss_B, n, sigma2_hat)

Adding s6 improves the fit by n·log(RSS_A/RSS_B) = 3.108 on the AIC/BIC log-likelihood scale, and by (RSS_A−RSS_B)/σ̂² = 3.029 on the Cp scale. AIC’s penalty for one extra parameter is just 2, and Cp’s is also 2 — both smaller than the 3.03–3.11 improvement, so both criteria judge s6 worth including. BIC’s penalty is log(n) = log(370) = 5.914, which is larger than the improvement, so BIC judges s6 not worth its complexity cost. That’s exactly why they disagree: same fit improvement, different bars for “is it worth it.”

Selecting a model this way never proves it’s the true data-generating model — it only shows that, under a particular penalty’s assumptions, one candidate balances fit and complexity better than another candidate you happened to compare it against. A different penalty, a different candidate set, or a different sample could favor a different model; none of these criteria test whether the chosen model’s functional form or included variables are actually correct.

Question 5: Validation and final test data

Use rows 1 through 370 of diabetes.csv as the training data and rows 371 through 442 as the final test data. Consider eleven nested candidate models. For m=0,1,…,10m=0,1,\ldots,10, the model with mm predictors contains an intercept and the first mm predictors in this order:

age, sex, bmi, bp, s1, s2, s3, s4, s5, s6.

An analyst proposes the following procedure:

  1. Fit all eleven candidate models using the training data.
  2. Calculate the MSE of each model on the final test data.
  3. Select the model with the smallest test MSE.
  4. Report that minimum as the final estimate of prediction error.

The analyst argues that the procedure is valid because the final test data were not used to estimate the regression coefficients.

  1. Identify the first step that misuses the final test data. Explain why the minimum of eleven test MSE values is generally too favorable as an estimate of the selected procedure’s future prediction error.

  2. Rewrite the analysis using five-fold cross-validation within the training data. State how the predictor count is selected, what is refitted, and when the final test data may be used.

  3. Suppose the analyst has already examined all eleven test MSE values. What can still be reported transparently, and what additional data would be needed for a new final evaluation?

Show the starter code 
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
 
# ============================================================
# Setup (shared across parts a, b, c)
# ============================================================
df = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
 
predictors = ["age", "sex", "bmi", "bp", "s1", "s2", "s3", "s4", "s5", "s6"]
 
train = df.iloc[:370].reset_index(drop=True)      # rows 1-370
final_test = df.iloc[370:442].reset_index(drop=True)  # rows 371-442
 
y_train_full = train["y"].to_numpy()
y_final_test = final_test["y"].to_numpy()
 
 
def design_matrix(data, m):
    """Intercept + the first m predictors, in the stated order."""
    cols = [np.ones(len(data))] + [data[predictors[j]].to_numpy() for j in range(m)]
    return np.column_stack(cols)
 
 
def fit_and_mse(X_fit, y_fit, X_eval, y_eval):
    coef, _, _, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(X_fit, y_fit, rcond=None)
    resid = y_eval - X_eval @ coef
    return np.mean(resid ** 2)
 
test_mse_by_m = np.empty(11)
for m in range(11):
    X_train_m = design_matrix(train, m)
    X_test_m = design_matrix(final_test, m)
    test_mse_by_m[m] = fit_and_mse(X_train_m, y_train_full, X_test_m, y_final_test)
 
best_m_flawed = int(np.argmin(test_mse_by_m))
 
print("=== Part (a): analyst's procedure ===")
for m in range(11):
    print(f"m={m:2d}, final-test MSE = {test_mse_by_m[m]:.3f}")
print(f"Selected m = {best_m_flawed}, reported 'final' MSE = {test_mse_by_m[best_m_flawed]:.3f}")
print("(This number is biased low -- see written explanation.)")
=== Part (a): analyst's procedure ===
m= 0, final-test MSE = 5822.890
m= 1, final-test MSE = 5527.791
m= 2, final-test MSE = 5527.210
m= 3, final-test MSE = 3719.235
m= 4, final-test MSE = 3246.823
m= 5, final-test MSE = 3234.919
m= 6, final-test MSE = 3207.615
m= 7, final-test MSE = 2636.502
m= 8, final-test MSE = 2624.924
m= 9, final-test MSE = 2369.344
m=10, final-test MSE = 2484.776
Selected m = 9, reported 'final' MSE = 2369.344
(This number is biased low -- see written explanation.)

The first step that misuses the final test data is step 2, not step 3. As soon as the analyst computes test MSE for all eleven models on the final test set, that data has already been used to compare candidates — even though it wasn’t used to fit coefficients, it’s now driving which model gets chosen. “I didn’t use it for fitting” doesn’t make it untouched; selection is itself a use of the data.

Why the reported minimum (2369.3 at m=9 in the code run above) is too optimistic: each of the eleven test MSEs contains its own random noise from that specific 72-row test sample. Taking the minimum across eleven noisy estimates systematically favors whichever model got a lucky draw — you’re not just picking the best model, you’re picking the best model and the luckiest noise realization simultaneously. Reporting that minimum as “the” prediction error confuses the best-case outcome of a search with an unbiased estimate of future performance.

Show the starter code 
n_train = len(train)
n_folds = 5
fold_size = n_train // n_folds  # 74, divides evenly
fold_id = np.repeat(np.arange(n_folds), fold_size)  # contiguous folds, fully reproducible
 
cv_mse_by_m = np.empty(11)
for m in range(11):
    fold_mses = np.empty(n_folds)
    for f in range(n_folds):
        val_mask = fold_id == f
        fit_mask = ~val_mask
 
        X_fit = design_matrix(train[fit_mask].reset_index(drop=True), m)
        y_fit = y_train_full[fit_mask]
        X_val = design_matrix(train[val_mask].reset_index(drop=True), m)
        y_val = y_train_full[val_mask]
 
        fold_mses[f] = fit_and_mse(X_fit, y_fit, X_val, y_val)
    cv_mse_by_m[m] = fold_mses.mean()
 
best_m_cv = int(np.argmin(cv_mse_by_m))
 
print("\n=== Part (b): five-fold CV within training data ===")
for m in range(11):
    print(f"m={m:2d}, average CV MSE = {cv_mse_by_m[m]:.3f}")
print(f"CV-selected predictor count: m = {best_m_cv}")

X_train_final_model = design_matrix(train, best_m_cv)
X_final_test_eval = design_matrix(final_test, best_m_cv)
honest_test_mse = fit_and_mse(X_train_final_model, y_train_full, X_final_test_eval, y_final_test)
 
print(f"Refit m={best_m_cv} model on all 370 training rows.")
print(f"Single, honest evaluation on the untouched final test data: MSE = {honest_test_mse:.3f}")

m= 1, average CV MSE = 5813.259
m= 2, average CV MSE = 5839.850
m= 3, average CV MSE = 3935.647
m= 4, average CV MSE = 3686.173
m= 5, average CV MSE = 3698.345
m= 6, average CV MSE = 3709.906

m= 8, average CV MSE = 3282.347

Refit m=10 model on all 370 training rows.
Single, honest evaluation on the untouched final test data: MSE = 2484.776

Split only the 370 training rows into 5 folds (contiguous blocks of 74 here). For each candidate m, fit on 4 folds and validate on the 5th, cycling through all 5; average the 5 validation MSEs. The predictor count is selected as the m with the smallest average CV MSE — here that’s m=10, not m=9 (the flawed procedure’s pick was itself an artifact of test-set noise). The chosen model is then refit once using all 370 training rows (more data = better final coefficients). The final test data (rows 371–442) is touched exactly once, at the very end, to evaluate that single already-chosen model — giving MSE=2484.8, a more trustworthy (and less flattering) number than the flawed procedure’s 2369.3.

                 honest final MSE:  2484.776

Once an analyst has looked at all eleven final-test MSE values, that data is no longer untouched — it can no longer support a valid “final” evaluation of the selected procedure. What can still be reported transparently is the full set of eleven values themselves, labeled explicitly as exploratory/already-inspected results, alongside a description of the CV-based selection this should have been. To get one genuinely valid final assessment now, you’d need a new, previously unseen dataset (or newly collected future observations) that no step of the model-selection process has touched, so a single evaluation on it isn’t contaminated by the earlier look. ## Reference
